title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic network validator under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts report safe outcomes for every paired episode: baseline_safe = 240/240 and guarded_safe = 240/240. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract the single shared LLM candidate passed deterministic validation in every task, so no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the paired contrast is degenerate. We present the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded results, a focused failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction: Translating high‑level operator intent into device configurations that preserve ordering, dependencies, and safety invariants is a central NetOps challenge. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows increasingly propose network change plans, but token‑level or human‑grade text metrics fail to capture the semantic correctness required for safe application (ordering constraints, transient invariants, protected resources). Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are executed against device images or simulators and scored by deterministic checks—reveals planning and execution failures not visible in text‑only tests. Generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipelines combine LLM generation with deterministic validation and automated repair and are a commonly proposed architectural guardrail. However, open experimental questions remain about when and how a verifier causally reduces unsafe applications under distribution shift and adversarial inputs, and how experimental semantics (e.g., shared vs independent generation per arm) affect paired causal contrasts. We preregistered a paired emulation study to measure the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) under clear adapter semantics and execution accounting, with fully archived artifacts to enable deterministic reconciliation.
sections.related_work: Recent work proposes executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks for LLM agents in NetOps to surface workflow and planning errors beyond textual fidelity; such benchmarks demonstrate the need for execution‑grounded scoring [1]. Research on automatic configuration and program repair has repeatedly used generate–validate patterns and reports high repair coverage on selected benchmark faults, while noting that verifier semantic breadth constrains outcomes [2,4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, and verifier integration as promising but still unproven at production scale [3,5]. Work on configuration analysis (e.g., Batfish evolution) establishes engineering precedent for deterministic verification in networking [6]. Our study differs by (a) preregistering a single, explicit paired estimand and shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, (b) executing in an emulation‑grounded closed loop, and (c) fully archiving per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to permit deterministic audit and interpretation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand — The experiment was preregistered under study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, defined as the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. The analysis procedure and bootstrap parameters were preregistered and executed by the registered paired analysis executor with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap seed = 1729).

Design, task corpus, and blocking — We used a paired design with exactly N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks. The task corpus was blocked into three strata: in‑distribution (60%, 144 tasks), distribution‑shift (20%, 48 tasks; novel topologies/vendors), and adversarial‑prompt (20%, 48 tasks). Tasks were generated deterministically by the registered task generator and included explicit initial states, required command sequences, and preservation constraints to create semantically demanding scenarios.

Model, adapter contract, and validator — Execution declared the model gpt-5-mini and used an adapter implementing shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each pair the adapter produced a single initial LLM generation that was reused by both the baseline and guarded episodes. The guarded pipeline used a deterministic network validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and was permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair attempt per task. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics a paired difference can only arise if the shared candidate fails validation or if the guarded repair modifies the final configuration relative to baseline.

Scoring, exclusions, and missingness treatment — Final outcomes were scored binarily (safe vs unsafe) by deterministic execution checks. Predeclared exclusions included pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator reports unsafe) and infra failures after allowed retries. The preregistered retry policy permitted up to two infra reruns per task; primary analysis excluded unrecoverable infra failures as specified.

Analysis plan — The primary analysis applied the paired binary executor to generate a paired contingency table, compute the paired risk difference, derive a bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and perform an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. Secondary analyses planned median repair counts and model‑call budgets by stratum and a sensitivity analysis treating flagged items as unsafe. All analysis parameters and outputs were archived for deterministic reconciliation.
sections.results:
Execution accounting — The run completed under the preregistered contract. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. Adapter audit confirms exactly one shared initial generation per pair (hosted model calls = 240), consistent with the shared_initial_candidate contract. No infra failures or unrecoverable errors occurred.

Primary binary outcomes — Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline_safe = 240/240 and guarded_safe = 240/240. The paired contingency is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 (guarded unsafe, baseline safe) = 0; n01 (baseline unsafe, guarded safe) = 0; n00 (both unsafe) = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity — No validator‑triggered repairs were applied during the run (repair_attempts = 0). Representative validator traces record the semantic difficulty labels and detailed final state snapshots used to assess safety, but every shared candidate passed the deterministic checks so the guarded pipeline had no occasion to alter outputs. Planned sensitivity channels for validator PASS vs emulator inconsistency and infra failures were unused because no such flags occurred.

Subgroup outcomes — The result pattern is identical across all strata (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial): zero unsafe applies in both arms. Consequently, subgroup paired contrasts are degenerate and provide no evidence of an arm difference under the executed semantics and adversary strength.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation of the null paired contrast — The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced a single LLM output per task that both arms consumed. Deterministic validation passed every shared candidate; consequently, the guarded arm did not invoke repairs and could not produce a discordant outcome. This mechanistic explanation—rooted in the adapter contract, provider call accounting, and validator traces—fully accounts for the observed contingency (n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = 0) and the statistical outputs (estimate = 0.0; CI = [0.0,0.0]; p = 1.0).

Design implications for informative GVR experiments — The shared_initial_candidate contract trades model‑call efficiency and exact pairing for an experiment that yields informative causal contrasts only when initial generations sometimes fail deterministic validation. When the goal is to estimate the causal effect of a verifier on final safety outcomes, experimental designs that permit generator variability between arms or that (a) increase adversary strength, (b) expand repair budgets, or (c) introduce controlled generator perturbations will be more likely to produce discordant pairs and therefore to measure verifier benefit. These recommendations are directly motivated by the observed provider‑call accounting and zero repair usage.

Threats to validity — Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate semantics is an explicit design choice that constrains causal interpretation; adherence to that contract is confirmed by audited model‑call counts. Construct validity: the deterministic validator encodes a finite check set and therefore may not capture all semantic fault classes; planned checks for validator PASS vs emulator outcome mismatch were available but not triggered. External validity: the task corpus is an emulation‑grounded synthetic benchmark; extrapolation to production, multi‑vendor deployments and operator workflows is limited. Conclusion validity: the observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 precludes demonstrating a verifier benefit in this experimental instantiation; power calculations conditional on higher baseline failure rates remain relevant for future designs.

Operational interpretation and recommendations — Do not interpret the null paired contrast as evidence that verifiers are universally unnecessary. Instead: (1) match generation semantics to the causal question—use independent initial generations per arm when testing verifier effect; (2) increase repair iteration budgets and instrument repair traces to study repair search behavior; (3) strengthen adversary protocols (adaptive adversaries, wider perturbations) to create validation opportunities; and (4) broaden verifier semantic coverage and add cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator execution to detect possible false‑safe outcomes. The archived execution accounting and validator traces provide concrete starting points to implement and measure these changes reproducibly.
sections.conclusion: We performed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. The concrete, artifact‑grounded outcome is that every paired episode was scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240; guarded = 240/240), producing a paired difference of zero with a degenerate bootstrap CI and McNemar p = 1.0. This null result is explained by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics: the single shared LLM candidate passed deterministic validation in all tasks and therefore the guarded pipeline had no occasion to apply repairs. The study illustrates how execution semantics and verifier coverage determine whether a GVR experiment will be informative and provides artifact‑grounded recommendations for future designs that aim to measure verifier causal benefit under distribution shift and adversarial probes.

disclosure_statement: Declared model and orchestration: execution used the declared hosted model 'gpt-5-mini' via the registered adapter family 'hosted_netops_gvr_v1'. Guardrail and repair contract: the guarded pipeline used a deterministic network validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Preregistration and autonomy boundary: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256 archived in the evidence bundle). The human Research Director selected the broad topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; all literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock per the track rules. Generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial LLM generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract the paired contrast could only differ if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. Master prompt archive: the immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba) and is provided as the required immutable locator. Reproducibility pointers: execution accounting, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle and referenced in the manuscript; readers may consult the archived execution manifest for machine‑verifiable provenance. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was exercised; results do not imply generality across other models, prompt templates, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: the deterministic validator implements a finite set of semantic checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected, and planned cross‑checks for validator PASS vs emulator mismatches were not triggered in this run.
